critique.good: ID and Title remain readable, and the table is almost phone-width, so it avoids serious horizontal scrolling.
critique.problems: Severity, Assignee, Status and Updated collapse into vertical letter stacks; headers and values split almost character by character; rows become 153–199px tall and the table reaches 1301px, so cross-row triage is impossible.
critique.cause: Columns 3–6 are only 38px wide, leaving 17px of text after 21px padding—below every header and word. The 119px Title is workable, but the four metadata columns are far below their minimums; total 367px also exceeds 359px.

critique.good: The most usable design: no mid-word splits, all headers fit on one line, ID/Severity/Assignee are at sensible exact widths, and the 589px table requires only moderate scrolling.
critique.problems: Status wraps 'In progress' onto two lines and Updated wraps relative times, producing uneven 60/83px rows; metadata feels cramped while Title has surplus width. The right side is still partly off-screen on a phone.
critique.cause: Status at 82px and Updated at 83px are below their one-line widths of 98px and 108px, while Title at 160px has spare room. The 588px total is only just above the theoretical 582px no-split minimum, so the problem is allocation, not total width.

critique.good: Every row is a clean 36px single line; headers and values stay intact, giving an excellent scanning rhythm in isolation.
critique.problems: At 885px the table is far too wide: the 360px viewport shows only ID and part of Title, while Severity, Assignee, Status and Updated are completely off-screen. Triage requires scrolling away from row identity.
critique.cause: Title is allocated 415px—almost half the table—despite a one-line width of 394px and a longest word of only 92px. The metadata columns are at full one-line widths, so the total balloons to 885px. This is the content overview, not a phone layout.

critique.good: Even, legible column rhythm; headers stay on one line; no mid-word splits; Title at 140px keeps rows from becoming extreme (only one 5-line row).
critique.problems: The table is 610px wide inside a 360px box — the reader must scroll past Assignee, Status and Updated to answer any triage question, and ID+Title alone (236px) barely fit, so the primary scan path is cramped while the columns that cause the overflow (Status 98, Updated 108) are the ones nobody needs first. Rows are also uneven (36/83/83/129/83/60/106) so the eye loses the row band.
critique.cause: Roughly 77px of pure slack in the fixed columns: ID 96 where 60 suffices (BUG-2041 is 39px), Status 98 where 82 suffices, Updated 108 where 83 suffices. Meanwhile Title is starved at 140px, forcing 3–5 line rows. The five non-Title columns sum to 469px, i.e. 109px more than the entire viewport, before Title is given anything at all.

critique.good: Slightly narrower total than r1A, and the Assignee header is fully visible with the name on one line.
critique.problems: Worst vertical result of the three: five of six body rows are 4–5 lines tall (106/83/129/106/83/129), so the table is 673px tall and no two issues can be compared without scrolling. The wasted ID/Status/Updated widths were not reclaimed — the 21px saved was simply taken out of Title.
critique.cause: Title cut to 119px (98px of text) while ID 96, Status 98, Updated 108 stayed fat. Title is the only column that actually needs more room and it got less, so line count exploded.

critique.good: Best vertical rhythm by far — rows are 2–3 lines (36/83/60/83/83/60/83) and the table is only 487px tall; Title reads as a phrase rather than a stack of words.
critique.problems: Still 630px wide, the worst overflow of the three. Enlarging Title was paid for entirely by extra scroll, so the reader sees ID, Title and Severity and must scroll for ownership, status and recency — the exact triage fields the table exists to show. The other five columns remain oversized.
critique.cause: Title 160 added 20px onto a fixed base of 469px that was never reduced. The base itself is the bug: 469 > 360 means no Title width could ever make this fit.

critique.good: Title at 190px gives the primary scan path room: most titles resolve in 2–3 lines, headers stay one line, no mid-word splits, and rows stay at 83px or less.
critique.problems: ID is too narrow: every BUG-2041 breaks into 'BUG-' / '2041', so the identifier no longer reads as one token and each row gains a line. At 583px wide, Assignee/Status/Updated are pushed off-screen.
critique.cause: ID is 60px, but BUG-2041 needs 75px of content plus 21px padding; total width 583px exceeds the 360px frame by 223px.

critique.good: Narrowest of the three at 543px, with all wraps at spaces and no mid-word splits. Metadata columns stay at their minimum unbreakable widths and headers remain one line.
critique.problems: Same ID split as r2A. Title at 150px is too tight: the UTC+13 row reaches four lines and 106px height, creating a tall, uneven vertical rhythm. Still overflows by 183px.
critique.cause: Title 150px leaves only 129px of content, below the comfortable width for long titles; ID at 60px is below the 75px one-line identifier width.

critique.good: Title at 220px is the most readable: long titles settle in 2–3 lines, rows are the shortest overall at 418px, headers stay one line, and there are no mid-word splits.
critique.problems: Widest table at 613px, so more triage columns are hidden. ID still splits 'BUG-' / '2041', meaning the row identity is broken while title is over-favored.
critique.cause: Title 220px plus ID 60px: the extra title width adds 30px over r2A with little row-height gain, while ID remains 15px short of its one-line width.

understanding.purpose: A phone-width issue tracker for scanning and triaging bugs: identify the issue, judge urgency/status, see ownership and recency.
understanding.reading: Readers scan top-down by row: ID and title locate the issue, then severity/status/assignee/updated answer triage questions. Cross-row comparison is mainly severity, status and recency.
groups: ID + Title: together form the row identity and the primary scan path
Severity + Status: both express triage state and are compared across rows
Assignee + Updated: secondary ownership and recency metadata, read after triage state
keep_intact: ID strings such as BUG-2041, including the hyphen
Severity and status values and their headers
may_wrap: Two-word status or updated values at spaces, not inside words

bad.why: Title is only 119px, forcing most issue titles into 4–5 lines and stretching rows to 106–129px; the table becomes 673px tall and the title column no longer scans as prose.
ID is only 60px, so every BUG-#### identifier breaks across two lines, undermining the key column just to widen Title.
Combines the ID fault of r2A with a still-too-narrow 150px Title, producing split identifiers and 4-line titles without gaining a coherent layout.
ID is split in every row while Title is over-allocated at 220px; the table still overflows and the most stable identifier is the least intact.
Title at 130px forces 5-line titles and 627px table height; the narrow prose column destroys the table’s vertical rhythm.

final.rationale: r1C is the cleanest compromise: ID stays on one line, and Severity, Assignee, Status and Updated each get exactly enough width for their one-line content, while Title wraps as prose to at most three lines. Its 630px width costs more horizontal scroll than r3A, but it avoids wrapping short metadata such as status and dates. r3A is close but starves Status and Updated below their one-line needs; r2A and r2C buy title width by breaking every BUG-#### identifier. The compressed-title designs (r1B, r2B, r3B) are clearly worse because they turn issue titles into tall stacks of words.

general: Give atomic columns—identifiers, dates, statuses—their one-line widths before allocating leftover space to prose columns.
A primary descriptive column should dominate the grid; equal widths or symmetry are not goals in a table like this.
Breaking an identifier across lines usually costs more scanning clarity than accepting horizontal scroll.
On narrow screens, a table that scrolls horizontally is often better than a false fit that fragments cells.
specific: Issue titles are prose and may wrap; BUG-#### identifiers should stay intact.
Severity, Assignee, Status and Updated are short metadata columns with one-line minima around 80, 87, 98 and 108px including padding.
At 360px this six-column issue tracker cannot fit, so the design decision is which columns remain intact.
Status and Updated widths below roughly 98px and 108px are likely to wrap values even when row heights hide it.

final.tradeoffs: A reasonable designer could prefer r3A or r2C for shorter rows and a wider Title, accepting wrapped metadata or split IDs. r1C deliberately spends about 30px more horizontal width than r3A to keep all non-title cells on one line.
final.uncertain: The actual Status and Updated strings are not visible in the overview, so it is uncertain whether r3A’s 82/83px columns merely wrap gracefully or visibly damage scanning; r1C’s 630px total may also feel like too much horizontal scroll on a phone.

A.why: IDs and severity remain intact, and most of the assignee column is visible initially. The narrow title column creates tall rows, and status and updated information require horizontal scrolling.

B.why: The wider title column keeps phrases together and makes rows easy to scan. IDs and severity are clear, though assignee and the remaining columns require scrolling.

C.why: Titles wrap naturally and remain readable, with intact IDs and severity values. The initial view reaches only the beginning of assignee, so the remaining fields require scrolling.

D.why: All columns fit, but headers, IDs, titles, names and dates break into fragments. The resulting tall rows are very difficult to scan or compare.

E.why: IDs and severity read clearly, but the title column produces more wrapping than B or C. Assignee is only partly visible and the remaining fields require scrolling.

F.why: Assignees fit and the initial view reaches status, but every ID breaks across lines and narrow titles make the rows tall. Status and updated information still require scrolling.

reviews.unsure: The images show only the left portion of the scrolling layouts, so the widths and readability of their off-screen status and updated columns cannot be assessed.

A.why: Everything fits in the viewport, but identifiers, headings, names and title words are broken into fragments. The very tall rows are difficult to scan.

B.why: IDs and severity values stay intact, and titles remain readable despite frequent wrapping. The viewport cuts through the assignee column, with later fields requiring scrolling.

C.why: The generous title column keeps most titles to two or three lines, and IDs and severity are easy to scan. Assignee and later fields require horizontal scrolling.

D.why: IDs and severity stay intact, and titles wrap naturally. The viewport shows only part of the assignee column, and the longer titles take several lines.

E.why: Assignee names fit within the viewport, but every ID breaks across two lines and the narrow title column makes several rows tall. Status is cut off at the viewport edge.

F.why: IDs and severity remain intact, while titles wrap into readable two- or three-line blocks. The viewport cuts through assignee, leaving the remaining fields to be reached by scrolling.

reviews.unsure: The provided images do not show the full width of the scrolling layouts, so the widths and readability of their later columns cannot be assessed directly. C's wider title column also means less of the assignee column is visible initially.

A.why: IDs and short fields stay intact and titles break at spaces, but Title is narrower than the over-wide Severity column, making many rows 4–6 lines tall; Assignee is cut at the right edge.

B.why: Best balance: compact ID, adequate Title, compact Severity, and no mid-word splits; only a thin sliver of Assignee shows at the right, so scrolling is required, but the visible reading order is clean.

C.why: Titles and IDs are readable, but ID and Severity are both much wider than their short contents need, pushing Assignee, Status and Updated entirely off-screen; wasteful use of the 360px.

D.why: All six columns are squeezed into tiny widths; IDs, titles, statuses and dates split mid-token (BUG-/204, progr/ess, 2024/-06-/02), making the table unreadable and untrustworthy.

E.why: Title gets the most room and Severity stays compact, so rows wrap reasonably; however the ID column is needlessly wide and Assignee/Status/Updated are off-screen, making it less efficient than B.

F.why: The ID splits across lines (BUG-/2041), Title is too narrow and turns rows into tall stacks, while Status is only a clipped sliver; width is spent on Assignee at the cost of the identifier and main text.

reviewsOld.unsure: Exact column widths are hard to measure from the screenshots, and I cannot verify whether the clipped right edge is intended as a horizontal-scroll affordance.

A.why: Everything is crushed into 360px: the ID splits into 'BUG / -204 / 1', headers break mid-word ('Seve rity', 'Assi gnee', 'Upd ated'), and Title words shatter ('Chec kout butto n unre spon sive'). Rows become towering columns of fragments; nothing scans.

B.why: Good instinct to protect Title and ID, but Title is given less width than the others in this group, wrapping to four lines ('Checkout button / unresponsive / on Safari 17' style), while Assignee is still cut at the dashed edge anyway — an inefficient trade.

C.why: ID, Title and Severity read cleanly; Title wraps at word boundaries in three lines and keeps a comfortable measure. Status/Updated fall outside the frame and the reader must scroll, but the primary reading column is intact, which is the right priority.

D.why: Same sensible trade as C: intact identifiers, a generous Title column with no broken words, Severity fully readable; the overflow is pushed to the peripheral columns. Reads well as far as it goes.

E.why: Fits five columns and shows Status, but the identifier breaks at the hyphen ('BUG- / 2041') and Title is squeezed enough to wrap into many short lines, weakening the row-as-unit reading. Status is still clipped, so the extra column buys little.

F.why: Balanced like C/D: ID intact, Title at a readable measure with word-level wrapping only, Severity and part of Assignee visible; the remaining columns are clearly off-frame rather than mangled.

reviewsOld.unsure: B/C/D/F look near-identical in width allocation, so the ranking among them rests on small differences in Title measure and how much of Assignee survives the dashed edge; I also can't tell whether the cut-off right column is an intended horizontal scroll or accidental overflow.
